analysis.one_liner: Hides fully paid or settled medical debts from consumer credit reports.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 61 House supporters and no opposition vote ever recorded, died in the Financial Services Committee without a hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Getting sick or hurt can land a person's medical bills with a collection agency, and even after those bills are fully paid off or settled, the record can stay on their credit report and drag down their credit score for years. This bill would change federal credit reporting law so that once a medical debt in collections is fully paid or settled, credit bureaus could not keep reporting it beyond 45 days. Millions of Americans carry medical debt, so the change would affect credit scores, mortgage approvals, and loan interest rates for a large share of households.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose medical debts went to collections and were then fully paid off or settled. The bill's findings cite roughly 73 million working-age adults affected by medical bill problems and 30 million contacted by a collection agency over unpaid medical bills in 2010. Their credit scores would recover sooner, making it easier to qualify for a mortgage, a car loan, or a credit card at a fair rate.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to bar credit bureaus from reporting a medical debt that had been in collection once it is fully paid or settled, beyond 45 days from the payment or settlement date.

The bill's own findings state that medical debt that has been completely paid off or settled can still significantly damage a credit score for years, causing consumers to be denied credit or pay higher interest rates on homes and credit cards.
The findings note that medical bills make up more than half of all non-credit-related collections reported to credit bureaus, so the change reaches a very large group of consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies would lose a category of data they sell to lenders, and collection agencies and debt buyers would lose one of their main tools for pressuring people to pay, since the threat of a credit report hit would fade once a debt is settled. Health care providers would retain somewhat less leverage to push patients toward quick payment.

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers medical debts that are fully paid or settled, so it offers no relief to people still carrying unpaid medical bills, who are often the ones most financially strained.

Lenders argue that credit reports should reflect all outstanding obligations so they can price risk; stripping paid medical collections removes information from underwriting, though the bill's findings cite credit evaluators saying medical collections are inconsistently reported and of questionable value in predicting future payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: a paid medical bill should not shadow someone's credit for years and block them from a mortgage. The cost falls on credit bureaus and collectors rather than on ordinary consumers, and lenders' concern about lost information is blunted by evidence in the bill itself that medical collections are a poor predictor of repayment. The bill's main weakness is that it helps only people who manage to pay off or settle the debt, not those still struggling.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2013 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the Medical Debt Responsibility Act on April 26, 2013, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill attracted 60 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote after the referral.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee without advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and medical debt collection firms kept the status quo, since paid-off medical debt remains on credit reports and collectors keep the credit-score leverage. Consumers with paid medical collections gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip fully paid or settled medical collections from credit reports.

for.name: 60 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all 60 were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred and which controlled whether it got a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat without action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 61 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Republican-led committee.

industries.note: Bureaus such as the national credit bureaus sell the collection data this bill would remove, and paid medical collections currently keep consumers' scores lower. Losing that data costs them a product feature but costs consumers higher rates.

industries.industry: Medical debt collection agencies and debt buyers
industries.note: Collectors rely on the threat of a credit report entry to push people to pay quickly; shielding settled debts from reports weakens that leverage. The bill's findings note providers increasingly turn debt over to outside collectors.
Providers use credit reporting consequences to secure patient payment, so removing paid collections from reports reduces that pressure, though it does not affect the underlying debt.

Lenders would see less data, but borrowers whose scores recover become more creditworthy customers, and the bill's findings cite credit evaluators calling medical collections a poor predictor of repayment.
